title: Water Balance: Hypothalamus, Pituitary and ADH
subtitle: How the hypothalamus and pituitary control hormone release, with ADH as the worked example
subject: Biology

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, the hypothalamus, the pituitary and water balance. Let's get into it.

scenes.caption: Water Balance: Hypothalamus, Pituitary and ADH

scenes.heading: Who decides how much you pee?
scenes.body: After a long, hot afternoon of sport you barely need the toilet. Drink a litre of water and within an hour you do.
scenes.callout: Your kidneys don't make that call. Your brain does.
scenes.caption: Urine output changes with hydration because the brain controls a kidney hormone.

voiceover.text: Picture a long afternoon of sport on a hot day. You sweat for hours, and you barely need the toilet the whole time. Then you get home, drink a litre of water, and within an hour you're queuing for the bathroom. Your kidneys didn't decide that on their own. The decision was made in your brain, by a small region called the hypothalamus, working with a pea sized gland just below it, the pituitary. So today we'll look at how that pair controls the release of hormones, and we'll use one hormone, A D H, as our worked example of how your body keeps its water in balance.

scenes.heading: The hypothalamus runs the pituitary
scenes.body: The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems, and it controls hormone release from the pituitary.

bullets.text: The hypothalamus monitors the blood and links the nervous system to the endocrine system.
Posterior pituitary: stores and releases hormones made in the hypothalamus, such as ADH.
Anterior pituitary: makes its own hormones when hypothalamic releasing hormones arrive.
Many pituitary hormones then control other glands, like the thyroid and adrenal glands.

scenes.callout: Hypothalamus gives the orders; the pituitary sends them out.
scenes.caption: The hypothalamus controls the posterior pituitary through nerves and the anterior pituitary through releasing hormones.

voiceover.text: So let's meet the control team. The hypothalamus sits at the base of the brain, and it constantly monitors the blood, things like temperature and how concentrated it is. It's also the main link between the nervous system and the endocrine system. Hanging just below it is the pituitary gland, which has two parts that work quite differently. The posterior pituitary doesn't make its own hormones. Nerve cells from the hypothalamus make hormones like A D H, send them down their fibres, and the posterior pituitary stores and releases them. The anterior pituitary does make its own hormones, but only when releasing hormones from the hypothalamus arrive through tiny blood vessels. And many of those anterior pituitary hormones go on to control other glands, like the thyroid and the adrenal glands, which is why the pituitary is called the master gland, even though it takes its orders from the hypothalamus.

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: Hypothalamus: brain region that detects changes in the blood and controls the pituitary.
Pituitary gland: the 'master gland' below the hypothalamus that releases hormones controlling other glands.
Osmoreceptors: cells in the hypothalamus that detect changes in blood solute concentration.
ADH (antidiuretic hormone): made in the hypothalamus, released by the posterior pituitary; increases water reabsorption.
Aquaporins: water channels that ADH adds to kidney tubule walls.

scenes.callout: Antidiuretic means against urine: more ADH, less urine.
scenes.caption: Hypothalamus, pituitary, osmoreceptors, ADH and aquaporins.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down the key terms. The hypothalamus is the brain region that detects changes in the blood and controls the pituitary. The pituitary gland is the so called master gland just below it, releasing hormones that control many other glands. Osmoreceptors are cells in the hypothalamus that detect changes in the concentration of solutes in the blood. A D H stands for antidiuretic hormone. It's made in the hypothalamus, released by the posterior pituitary, and it increases water reabsorption in the kidney. And aquaporins are the water channels that A D H adds to the walls of the kidney tubules. The name antidiuretic is a handy clue, because it means against urine. More A D H, less urine.

scenes.heading: ADH: a hypothalamus and pituitary loop
scenes.body: When the blood becomes too concentrated, the hypothalamus triggers ADH release and the kidney reclaims water.

bullets.text: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect blood that is too concentrated.
The posterior pituitary releases ADH into the blood.
ADH adds aquaporins to the distal tubule and collecting duct, so more water is reabsorbed.
Blood concentration falls, and ADH release is switched down: negative feedback.

scenes.secondary: High ADH gives a small volume of concentrated urine. Low ADH gives a large volume of dilute urine.
scenes.callout: More ADH, more aquaporins, more water saved.
scenes.caption: Concentrated blood, osmoreceptors, ADH from the posterior pituitary, aquaporins, water reabsorbed.

voiceover.text: Now let's watch the team in action with A D H. It starts when your blood becomes too concentrated, maybe from sweating, salty food or not drinking. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect that change, and the hypothalamus sends signals down its nerve fibres to the posterior pituitary, which releases A D H into the blood. A D H travels to the kidneys, where it acts on the last parts of the nephron, the distal tubule and especially the collecting duct. It makes the cells there add aquaporins to their walls, so more water moves out of the filtrate and back into the blood. As the blood becomes less concentrated, the osmoreceptors stop firing as strongly, and A D H release drops. That's negative feedback. So high A D H gives you a small volume of concentrated urine, and low A D H gives you lots of dilute urine.

scenes.heading: Trace the dehydration response
scenes.question: A person becomes dehydrated on a hot day. Describe the homeostatic response that restores blood concentration, naming the stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector and response.
scenes.coachNote: Build the loop in order, and name where ADH is made, where it is released and where it acts.
steps: Stimulus: water loss makes the blood too concentrated.
Receptor: osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the change.
Control centre: the hypothalamus, which makes ADH and signals the posterior pituitary to release it.
Effector and response: kidney tubules add aquaporins, water is reabsorbed and urine becomes concentrated.
Negative feedback: blood concentration returns to normal, so ADH release falls ✓
scenes.caption: Dehydration: osmoreceptors, hypothalamus, ADH from the posterior pituitary, kidney reabsorbs water.

voiceover.text: Let's trace the dehydration response in full, the classic pathway question. The stimulus first. On a hot day you lose water, so your blood becomes too concentrated. The receptor is the osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus, which detect that rise. The control centre is the hypothalamus itself. It makes A D H and signals the posterior pituitary to release it into the blood. Now the effector and the response, and here you must be specific. The kidney tubules, especially the collecting ducts, add aquaporins, water is reabsorbed back into the blood, and the urine becomes small in volume and concentrated. Finish by naming the feedback type. It's negative feedback, because the response lowers blood concentration, which is the opposite of the original change, and A D H release then falls.

scenes.heading: Reading hormone data
scenes.body: Illustrative data: a person drinks 1 L of water at time 0.

bullets.text: Blood solute concentration falls, so ADH levels fall.
As ADH falls, urine output rises sharply.
Once the extra water is removed, ADH and urine output return towards normal.

scenes.callout: ADH and urine output move in opposite directions.
scenes.caption: After drinking water, ADH falls and urine output rises; both recover as balance returns.

voiceover.text: Now the syllabus wants you to read hormone data, so let's try some. These are illustrative numbers for a person who drinks a litre of water at time zero. Look at the blood concentration column first. It drops from two hundred and ninety to two hundred and eighty one by sixty minutes, because the water dilutes the blood. Over the same time, A D H falls from two and a half to half a picogram per millilitre, and urine output climbs from one to twelve millilitres a minute. So as A D H goes down, urine output goes up, an inverse relationship, which is exactly what you'd predict from fewer aquaporins. Then by a hundred and twenty minutes, the extra water has gone, blood concentration is back up, A D H has risen again and urine output has fallen. That return to normal is negative feedback, showing up in data.

scenes.heading: Three traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: saying ADH is made in the pituitary. ADH is made in the hypothalamus, then stored in and released from the posterior pituitary.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: calling the pituitary the boss. It is the master gland for other glands, but the hypothalamus controls it. Trap 3: saying ADH increases urine. Antidiuretic means against urine, so more ADH means less, more concentrated urine.
scenes.callout: Made in the hypothalamus. Released by the pituitary. More ADH, less urine.
scenes.caption: ADH is made in the hypothalamus, released by the posterior pituitary, and reduces urine volume.

voiceover.text: Three traps, and they come up every year. Trap one, saying A D H is made in the pituitary. Be precise. A D H is made by nerve cells in the hypothalamus, then stored in and released from the posterior pituitary, so keep the site where it's made separate from the site of release. Trap two, calling the pituitary the boss of the whole system. It is the master gland for many other glands, but the hypothalamus controls the pituitary, so the hypothalamus sits at the top. Trap three, mixing up the direction. A D H does not increase urine. Antidiuretic means against urine, so more A D H means less urine, and that urine is more concentrated.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: A person drinks two litres of water quickly, so blood osmolarity falls below normal. What happens to ADH secretion, the collecting duct, and the urine produced?
scenes.pausePrompt: Pause and run the loop the other way.
answerSteps: Stimulus: blood becomes too dilute (solute concentration falls).
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect this, so the posterior pituitary releases less ADH.
With little ADH, few aquaporins are inserted and the collecting duct reabsorbs less water.
A large volume of dilute urine is produced, bringing blood concentration back to normal.
Answer: ADH falls, less water reabsorbed, dilute high-volume urine ✓
scenes.caption: Overhydration: ADH falls, duct impermeable, dilute high-volume urine.

voiceover.text: Quick check, and this time we run the loop the other way. A person drinks two litres of water quickly, so their blood becomes too dilute. What happens to A D H secretion, the collecting duct, and the urine produced? Pause and reason it through. Right, let's check it. The stimulus is blood that's too dilute. The osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect that, so less A D H is released from the posterior pituitary. With very little A D H around, fewer aquaporins are inserted, so the collecting duct lets much less water back into the blood. That means the person produces a large volume of dilute urine, removing the extra water and bringing blood concentration back to normal. So A D H falls, less water is reabsorbed, and you get lots of dilute urine. Same negative feedback loop, just running the other way.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: The hypothalamus monitors the blood and controls the pituitary gland.
The posterior pituitary releases hormones made in the hypothalamus; the anterior pituitary makes its own when signalled.
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect blood that is too concentrated or too dilute.
ADH adds aquaporins in the kidney tubules, so more water is reabsorbed.
High ADH: small concentrated urine. Low ADH: large dilute urine. Negative feedback.
scenes.finalPrompt: Hormone question? Ask what is detected, where the hormone is made, where it is released, and what the effector does.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: hypothalamus in charge, two parts of the pituitary, osmoreceptors, ADH and aquaporins, feedback.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five takeaways. First, the hypothalamus monitors the blood and controls the pituitary gland. Second, the posterior pituitary releases hormones that are made in the hypothalamus, while the anterior pituitary makes its own hormones when the hypothalamus signals it. Third, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect whether the blood is too concentrated or too dilute. Fourth, A D H makes the kidney tubules add aquaporins, so more water is reabsorbed. And fifth, high A D H means a little concentrated urine, low A D H means lots of dilute urine, and the whole thing runs on negative feedback. For any hormone question, ask what's detected, where the hormone is made and released, and what the effector does.
